title: Contains Duplicate
statement: Given a list of integers, return True if any value appears at least twice, and False if every value is distinct.
hints: Checking 'x in list' inside a loop is O(n) each time.
A set remembers what you have seen in O(1) per lookup.
notes: Seen-set: O(n) time, O(n) space. Sorting first gives O(n log n) time and O(1) extra space if you may modify the input.

title: Two Sum
statement: Given a list of integers nums and an integer target, return the indices [i, j] with i < j such that nums[i] + nums[j] == target. Exactly one such pair exists. Do not use the same element twice.
hints: For each x, which value do you need to have seen already?
Store value -> index in a dict, and check before inserting.
notes: One pass with a dict: O(n) time, O(n) space. The brute force over all pairs is O(n^2).

title: Group Anagrams
statement: Given a list of lowercase words, group the words that are anagrams of each other. Return a list of groups (a list of lists). The order of the groups and of the words inside a group does not matter.

cases.name: example
cases.code: r = group_anagrams(['eat', 'tea', 'tan', 'ate', 'nat', 'bat']); assert sorted(sorted(g) for g in r) == [['ate', 'eat', 'tea'], ['bat'], ['nat', 'tan']]

cases.name: all the same group
cases.code: r = group_anagrams(['abc', 'cab', 'bca']); assert len(r) == 1 and sorted(r[0]) == ['abc', 'bca', 'cab']

hints: Two words are anagrams if they have the same letters. What key is the same for both?
A tuple of sorted letters is hashable; use it as a dict key.
notes: O(n * k log k) for n words of length k (sorting each word). Counting letters instead gives O(n * k).

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
statement: Given an unsorted list of integers, return the length of the longest run of consecutive integers (such as 4, 5, 6, 7) that can be formed from its values. Your solution must run in O(n) time.
hints: Sorting is O(n log n). Can a set answer 'is x - 1 present?' in O(1)?
Only start counting from a number whose predecessor is missing.
notes: Each run is walked once, from its start: O(n) time, O(n) space.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
statement: Given a list of integers nums and an integer k, return how many contiguous, non-empty subarrays have a sum equal to k. Values may be negative.
hints: The sum of nums[i:j] is prefix[j] - prefix[i].
Keep a dict of how many times each prefix sum has occurred.
solution:
def subarray_sum(nums, k):
    seen, total, count = {0: 1}, 0, 0
    for x in nums:
        total += x
        count += seen.get(total - k, 0)
        seen[total] = seen.get(total, 0) + 1
    return count
notes: Prefix sums with a dict: O(n) time, O(n) space.

title: Valid Parentheses
statement: Given a string containing only the characters ()[]{}, return True if the brackets are balanced: every opening bracket is closed by the same type, in the correct order.
hints: Which bracket must be closed first? The most recent unresolved one.
A stack holds the openers; check the top when you see a closer.
notes: A stack: O(n) time, O(n) space.

title: Min Stack
statement: Design a stack class MinStack with push(x), pop(), top() and get_min(), where get_min() returns the smallest value currently in the stack. Every operation must take O(1) time.

cases.name: min after pushes
cases.code: s = MinStack(); s.push(5); s.push(3); s.push(7); assert s.get_min() == 3 and s.top() == 7

cases.name: min after pops
cases.code: s = MinStack(); [s.push(x) for x in (5, 3, 7)]; s.pop(); s.pop(); assert s.get_min() == 5

cases.name: duplicate minimums
cases.code: s = MinStack(); s.push(2); s.push(2); s.pop(); assert s.get_min() == 2

cases.name: increasing then decreasing
cases.code: s = MinStack(); [s.push(x) for x in (1, 2, 3, 0)]; assert s.get_min() == 0; s.pop(); assert s.get_min() == 1

cases.name: many operations are fast

hints: The minimum changes only when you push a smaller value or pop the current minimum.
Keep a second stack of running minimums.
notes: Two stacks: O(1) per operation, O(n) space.

title: Daily Temperatures
statement: Given a list of daily temperatures, return a list where answer[i] is the number of days you have to wait after day i to get a warmer temperature. If there is no warmer day, answer[i] is 0.

cases.name: 100,000 days must be fast (O(n))
cases.code: r = daily_temperatures(list(range(100000, 0, -1))); assert r[0] == 0 and len(r) == 100000

hints: Keep a stack of indices of days that are still waiting for a warmer day.
When today is warmer than the day on top of the stack, pop it and record the distance.
notes: A monotonic stack: each index is pushed and popped once, O(n).

title: Reverse a Linked List
statement: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list and return the new head. Do it in place with O(1) extra space.
hints: Walk the list and flip each next pointer to point backwards.
Save node.next before you overwrite it.
solution:
def reverse_list(head):
    prev = None
    while head:
        nxt = head.next
        head.next = prev
        prev, head = head, nxt
    return prev
notes: O(n) time, O(1) space.

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
statement: Given the heads of two sorted linked lists, merge them into one sorted list by relinking the existing nodes, and return its head.
hints: A dummy head node removes the special case for the first node.
Attach the smaller head each time and advance that list.
notes: O(n + m) time, O(1) extra space.

title: Linked List Cycle
statement: Given the head of a linked list, return True if the list contains a cycle (some node's next points back to an earlier node), otherwise False. Use O(1) extra space.
hints: A set of visited nodes works but uses O(n) space.
Two pointers moving at different speeds meet inside a cycle.
notes: Floyd's slow and fast pointers: O(n) time, O(1) space.

title: Remove the N-th Node From the End
statement: Given the head of a linked list and an integer n, remove the n-th node from the end of the list and return the head. n is always valid. Try to do it in one pass.
hints: Two pointers n nodes apart: when the fast one reaches the end, the slow one is just before the target.
A dummy head handles removing the first node.
notes: One pass: O(n) time, O(1) space.

title: Search Insert Position
statement: Given a sorted list of distinct integers and a target, return the index of the target if it is present, or the index where it would be inserted to keep the list sorted. Your solution must be O(log n).
hints: Binary search keeps lo and hi; the answer is where lo ends up.
Use lo <= hi with mid + 1 and mid - 1 so the range always shrinks.
notes: Binary search: O(log n). Python's bisect.bisect_left does the same.

title: Merge Intervals
statement: Given a list of intervals [start, end], merge all overlapping intervals and return the merged list sorted by start. Intervals that touch (such as [1, 4] and [4, 5]) count as overlapping.
hints: Sort by start first.
Compare the next start with the end of the last merged interval.
notes: Sorting dominates: O(n log n) time.

title: Minimum Eating Speed
statement: There are piles of bananas, piles[i] bananas in pile i, and h hours to eat them all. Each hour you choose one pile and eat up to k bananas from it (if the pile has fewer than k you eat all of it and waste the rest of the hour). Return the smallest integer k that finishes all piles within h hours. h is at least the number of piles.
hints: If speed k works, any larger speed also works. That is a monotonic yes/no question.
Binary search the speed between 1 and max(piles); a check is O(n).
notes: Binary search on the answer: O(n log max(piles)).

title: First and Last Position
statement: Given a sorted list of integers (possibly with duplicates) and a target, return [first_index, last_index] of the target, or [-1, -1] if it is absent. Your solution must be O(log n).
hints: bisect_left gives the first position of target.
bisect_right minus one gives the last position.
notes: Two binary searches: O(log n).

title: Maximum Depth of a Binary Tree
statement: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. The depth of an empty tree is 0.
hints: The depth of a node is 1 plus the larger depth of its children.
The base case is an empty tree: 0.
notes: O(n) time, O(h) stack space.

title: Level Order Traversal
statement: Given the root of a binary tree, return its values level by level, left to right, as a list of lists.
hints: Breadth-first search uses a queue.
Process len(queue) nodes at a time to separate the levels.
solution:
from collections import deque

def level_order(root):
    out, q = [], deque([root] if root else [])
    while q:
        level = []
        for _ in range(len(q)):
            node = q.popleft()
            level.append(node.val)
            q.extend(c for c in (node.left, node.right) if c)
        out.append(level)
    return out
notes: O(n) time, O(width) space.

title: Validate a Binary Search Tree
statement: Given the root of a binary tree, return True if it is a valid binary search tree: for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are larger (strictly).

examples.note: 3 is in the right subtree of 5 but smaller than 5

cases.name: invalid deeper down
cases.code: assert is_valid_bst(build_tree([5, 1, 4, None, None, 3, 6])) is False

cases.name: parent-child check is not enough
cases.code: assert is_valid_bst(build_tree([10, 5, 15, None, None, 6, 20])) is False

hints: Comparing a node only with its direct children misses violations deeper down.
Pass a lower and an upper bound down the recursion.
notes: O(n) time, O(h) stack space. An in-order traversal that checks for strictly increasing values also works.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor in a BST
statement: Given the root of a binary search tree with distinct values and two values p and q that are both in the tree, return the value of their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both p and q in its subtree (a node counts as its own descendant).
hints: Use the BST property: if both values are smaller than the node, go left.
The first node where p and q are on different sides (or equal to it) is the answer.
notes: O(h) time, O(1) space.

title: Number of Islands
statement: Given a grid of '1' (land) and '0' (water) as a list of strings, return the number of islands. An island is a group of land cells connected horizontally or vertically.
hints: Treat each land cell as a node and its four neighbours as edges.
Start a search from every unvisited land cell and count the starts. Use a visited set.
notes: O(rows x cols). The version here uses an explicit stack, so deep islands cannot hit Python's recursion limit.

title: Shortest Path in a Grid
statement: Given a square grid of 0 (open) and 1 (blocked), return the length of the shortest path from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell, counted in cells, moving up, down, left or right through open cells. Return -1 if there is no path.
hints: The fewest steps with equal costs is a breadth-first search.
Store the distance with each queued cell and mark cells seen when you enqueue them.
notes: BFS: O(rows x cols).

title: Course Schedule
statement: There are n courses numbered 0 to n-1. prerequisites is a list of pairs [a, b] meaning you must take course b before course a. Return True if it is possible to finish all courses (the prerequisites contain no cycle).

cases.name: long chain must be fast
cases.code: assert can_finish(20000, [[i + 1, i] for i in range(19999)]) is True

hints: Model courses as nodes and prerequisites as directed edges. A valid order exists exactly when there is no cycle.
Repeatedly take courses with no remaining prerequisites (Kahn's algorithm) and count them.
notes: Kahn's algorithm: O(n + edges). A DFS with three colours works too.

title: Kth Largest Element
statement: Given a list of integers and an integer k (1 <= k <= len(nums)), return the k-th largest element in sorted order (not the k-th distinct element). Aim for O(n log k) time.
hints: A min-heap of size k holds the k largest values seen so far.
Its root is the k-th largest.
notes: O(n log k) time, O(k) space.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
statement: Given a list of integers and an integer k, return the k most frequent values, in any order. The answer is guaranteed to be unique.

cases.name: 100,000 items
cases.code: assert sorted(top_k_frequent([i % 1000 for i in range(100000)] + [7] * 50, 1)) == [7]

hints: Count first (collections.Counter).
Then take the k values with the highest counts: a heap or Counter.most_common.
notes: O(n log k): one counting pass, then a heap of size k.

title: Merge K Sorted Lists
statement: Given a list of k sorted Python lists, merge them into one sorted list. Use a heap so the running time is O(N log k) for N total elements.

cases.name: many lists must be fast
cases.code: assert merge_k([[i, i + 1000] for i in range(1000)]) == sorted(sum([[i, i + 1000] for i in range(1000)], []))

hints: Push the first element of each list into a heap, with the list and position.
Pop the smallest, then push the next element from the same list.
solution:
import heapq

def merge_k(lists):
    heap = [(lst[0], i, 0) for i, lst in enumerate(lists) if lst]
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    out = []
    while heap:
        val, i, j = heapq.heappop(heap)
        out.append(val)
        if j + 1 < len(lists[i]):
            heapq.heappush(heap, (lists[i][j + 1], i, j + 1))
    return out
notes: O(N log k) time, O(k) heap.

title: Last Stone Weight
statement: You have a list of stone weights. Repeatedly take the two heaviest stones and smash them together: if they weigh the same both are destroyed, otherwise the lighter is destroyed and the heavier loses that much weight. Return the weight of the last remaining stone, or 0 if none remain.
hints: You always need the largest values: a max-heap.
heapq is a min-heap: push negated weights.
notes: O(n log n).

title: Subsets
statement: Given a list of distinct integers, return all possible subsets (the power set), in any order. The empty subset is included.

cases.name: all subsets are distinct
cases.code: r = subsets([1, 2, 3, 4]); assert len({tuple(sorted(s)) for s in r}) == 16

hints: For each element you either take it or skip it.
When you record a result, append a copy of the current path.
notes: O(n * 2^n): there are 2^n subsets and copying each costs up to n.

title: Permutations
statement: Given a list of distinct integers, return all possible orderings (permutations) of its elements, in any order.
hints: Choose one unused element at each position.
Mark an element used, recurse, then unmark it (undo).

title: Combination Sum
statement: Given a list of distinct positive integers (candidates) and a target, return every unique combination of candidates that sums to the target. A candidate may be used any number of times. Combinations may be returned in any order, and [2, 3] and [3, 2] count as the same combination.
hints: Sort the candidates so you can stop as soon as one is larger than what remains.
To avoid permutations of the same combination, only choose candidates at or after the current index.
notes: Exponential in the worst case; pruning cuts it a great deal in practice.

title: Generate Parentheses
statement: Given n pairs of parentheses, return all strings of well-formed (balanced) parentheses of length 2n, in any order.

cases.name: all are balanced
cases.code: assert all(s.count('(') == 4 for s in generate_parentheses(4))

hints: Add '(' while fewer than n have been used.
Add ')' only while the number of closings is smaller than the number of openings.
notes: The count is the Catalan number: roughly 4^n / n^1.5 strings.

title: Climbing Stairs
statement: You are climbing a staircase of n steps. Each move you climb 1 or 2 steps. Return the number of distinct ways to reach the top.

cases.name: n = 45 must be fast (no plain recursion)

hints: The ways to reach step i are the ways to reach i - 1 plus the ways to reach i - 2.
You only need the last two values.
notes: Fibonacci: O(n) time, O(1) space. Plain recursion without caching is exponential.

title: House Robber
statement: You are given the amount of money in each house along a street. You cannot rob two adjacent houses. Return the maximum amount you can rob.
hints: At each house: rob it (and add the best up to two houses back) or skip it.
Two variables are enough.
notes: O(n) time, O(1) space.

title: Coin Change
statement: Given a list of coin values and an amount, return the fewest coins needed to make that amount, or -1 if it is impossible. You have an unlimited supply of each coin.
hints: Let dp[a] be the fewest coins for amount a.
dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - c]) over coins c that fit.
notes: O(amount x coins) time, O(amount) space.

title: Longest Common Subsequence
statement: Given two strings, return the length of their longest common subsequence: the longest sequence of characters that appears in both in the same order (not necessarily contiguous).
hints: Let dp[i][j] be the answer for the first i and j characters.
If the characters match, add 1 to dp[i-1][j-1]; otherwise take the larger of dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1].
notes: O(m x n) time and space (space can drop to O(min(m, n)) keeping one row).

title: Edit Distance
statement: Given two strings, return the minimum number of single-character operations (insert, delete or replace) needed to turn the first into the second.
hints: dp[i][j] is the distance between the first i characters of a and the first j of b.
If the characters match, copy the diagonal; otherwise 1 + the minimum of insert, delete and replace.
notes: O(m x n) time and space.

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
statement: Given a string, return the length of the longest substring that contains no repeated character.
hints: Keep a window [left, right] with no repeats.
Remember the last index of each character; when a repeat appears inside the window, move left past it.
notes: Sliding window: O(n) time, O(alphabet) space.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell
statement: Given a list of daily prices, you may buy once and sell once on a later day. Return the maximum profit, or 0 if no profit is possible.
hints: For each day, the best profit selling today is price - the lowest price so far.
One pass, tracking the minimum so far.
notes: O(n) time, O(1) space.

title: Container With Most Water
statement: Given a list of non-negative heights representing vertical lines at positions 0, 1, 2, ..., choose two lines that, together with the x-axis, hold the most water. Return that maximum area (width between the lines times the shorter height).
hints: Start with the widest container: pointers at both ends.
Moving the taller line inward can never help. Move the shorter one.
notes: Two pointers: O(n) time, O(1) space.

title: Valid Anagram
statement: Given two strings s and t, return True if t is an anagram of s (the same letters with the same counts, in any order), otherwise False.
hints: If the lengths differ the answer is already False.
Count each letter. Two strings are anagrams exactly when the counts are equal.
notes: Counting: O(n) time, O(k) space for k distinct characters. Sorting both strings is O(n log n) and needs no extra structure. Ask whether the input is only lowercase ASCII (a 26-slot array) or Unicode (a hash map).

title: Product of Array Except Self
statement: Given a list of integers nums, return a list answer where answer[i] is the product of every element of nums except nums[i]. Do not use division, and aim for O(n) time.

examples.note: a zero makes every other product zero

hints: The product to the left of i times the product to the right of i is the answer.
Fill the answer with left products in one pass, then multiply by a running right product in a second pass.
solution:
def product_except_self(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    out = [1] * n
    left = 1
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = left
        left *= nums[i]
    right = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        out[i] *= right
        right *= nums[i]
    return out
notes: Prefix and suffix products: O(n) time, O(1) extra space besides the output. Dividing the total by nums[i] fails when a zero is present, which is why the problem forbids it.

title: Maximum Subarray
statement: Given a non-empty list of integers, return the largest sum of any contiguous (touching) run of elements.

examples.note: all negative: take the largest single value

cases.name: best run is in the middle

hints: At each position decide: extend the run that ends here, or start a new run at this element.
best ending here = max(x, best ending here + x). Keep the largest value seen.
notes: Kadane's algorithm: O(n) time, O(1) space. A common mistake is to start the best at 0, which returns the wrong answer when every value is negative.

title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
statement: Evaluate an arithmetic expression given as a list of tokens in reverse Polish notation. Operators are "+", "-", "*" and "/". Division truncates toward zero. Every expression is valid.
hints: Push numbers on a stack. An operator pops two values and pushes the result.
The first value popped is the right operand. Use int(a / b) so division truncates toward zero, not floor division.
notes: One pass, O(n) time and O(n) space. Python floor division (//) rounds -3.5 down to -4, so int(a / b) is used to truncate toward zero. Ask the interviewer which rounding is expected.

title: Sliding Window Maximum
statement: Given a list nums and a window size k, return the maximum of every window of k consecutive elements as the window moves from the left end to the right end.
hints: Recomputing max() for every window is O(n*k), too slow.
Keep a deque of indices whose values are in decreasing order. Drop indices that left the window from the front, and smaller values from the back before adding the new one.
notes: Monotonic deque: each index is added and removed at most once, so O(n) time and O(k) space. A heap with lazy deletion also works in O(n log n).

title: Add Two Numbers
statement: Two non-empty linked lists hold the digits of two non-negative integers in reverse order (the head is the ones digit). Return the sum as a linked list in the same format.

cases.name: final carry makes a new node

hints: Walk both lists together, adding the two digits and the carry. The new digit is total % 10, the new carry is total // 10.
Keep going while either list has nodes or the carry is not zero. A dummy head makes the first node no special case.
solution:
def add_two_numbers(l1, l2):
    dummy = cur = ListNode()
    carry = 0
    while l1 or l2 or carry:
        total = carry
        if l1:
            total += l1.val
            l1 = l1.next
        if l2:
            total += l2.val
            l2 = l2.next
        carry, digit = divmod(total, 10)
        cur.next = ListNode(digit)
        cur = cur.next
    return dummy.next
notes: O(max(m, n)) time, O(1) extra space besides the result. Converting to integers works in Python but defeats the point, and would not work in languages with fixed-size integers.

title: 3Sum
statement: Return all unique triplets [a, b, c] from nums such that a + b + c == 0. The result must not contain duplicate triplets. The order of triplets and of numbers inside a triplet does not matter.

cases.name: example
cases.code: assert sorted(sorted(t) for t in three_sum([-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4])) == [[-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]

cases.name: all zeros gives one triplet
cases.code: assert sorted(sorted(t) for t in three_sum([0, 0, 0, 0])) == [[0, 0, 0]]

cases.name: no duplicate triplets
cases.code:
r = three_sum([-2, 0, 0, 2, 2])
assert sorted(sorted(t) for t in r) == [[-2, 0, 2]]

hints: Sort the list. Fix the first number, then look for a pair that sums to its negative with two pointers.
Skip equal values for the first number and, after finding a triplet, skip equal values for the other two so that no duplicate is produced.
notes: Sort then two pointers: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space beyond the output and the sort. Say why: sorting is what makes the two-pointer step valid and makes duplicates easy to skip.

title: Binary Search
statement: Given a list of integers sorted in ascending order and a target, return the index of the target, or -1 if it is not in the list. The running time must be O(log n).

cases.name: 2,000,000 items need O(log n)

hints: Keep a low and a high index. Look at the middle, then throw away the half that cannot contain the target.
Loop while low <= high, and move to mid + 1 or mid - 1 so the range always shrinks.
notes: O(log n) time, O(1) space. Most binary search bugs are off by one: decide whether the range is closed [lo, hi] or half-open [lo, hi) and keep to it. In languages with fixed-size integers write lo + (hi - lo) // 2 to avoid overflow.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
statement: A list of distinct integers sorted in ascending order was rotated at an unknown pivot, for example [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7] became [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]. Return the index of target, or -1. The running time must be O(log n).

cases.name: 1,000,000 items need O(log n)

hints: At every step, one half of the range is still sorted. Find out which.
If the target lies inside the sorted half, search that half. Otherwise search the other one.
notes: O(log n) time. The key sentence for the interviewer: "after splitting at mid, at least one half is sorted, and I can tell whether the target is in that half by comparing it to the ends". With duplicates this can degrade to O(n).

title: Diameter of Binary Tree
statement: Return the length of the diameter of a binary tree: the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes. The path may or may not pass through the root.

cases.name: a long chain
cases.code:
root = TreeNode(0)
cur = root
for i in range(1, 800):
    cur.left = TreeNode(i)
    cur = cur.left
assert diameter(root) == 799

hints: For each node, the longest path through it is the height of its left subtree plus the height of its right subtree.
Compute heights bottom up and update a best-so-far value as you go, so you visit each node once.
notes: O(n) time, O(h) stack space where h is the height. Computing the height separately at every node is O(n^2) in the worst case, which is the usual first attempt.

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
statement: Imagine standing on the right side of a binary tree. Return the values of the nodes you can see, ordered from top to bottom.
hints: Do a level-order (breadth-first) traversal.
The last node of each level is the one you see from the right.
notes: O(n) time, O(w) space where w is the maximum width. A depth-first search that visits the right child first and records the first node seen at each depth gives the same answer.

title: Rotting Oranges
statement: A grid holds 0 (empty), 1 (fresh orange) and 2 (rotten orange). Every minute, each fresh orange next to a rotten one (up, down, left, right) becomes rotten. Return the number of minutes until no fresh orange is left, or -1 if that is impossible.

examples.note: the orange in the bottom-left corner is never reached

cases.name: 300 x 300 grid must be fast
cases.code:
g = [[1] * 300 for _ in range(300)]
g[0][0] = 2
assert oranges_rotting(g) == 598

hints: Start the search from all rotten oranges at the same time. That is a multi-source breadth-first search.
Process the queue one minute (one level) at a time. At the end, if any fresh orange is left, return -1.
notes: BFS: O(rows * cols) time and space. Do not mutate the caller's grid unless the interviewer allows it, which is why this uses a seen set.

title: Number of Provinces
statement: There are n cities. is_connected[i][j] is 1 if city i and city j are directly connected, 0 otherwise (and is_connected[i][i] is 1). A province is a group of cities connected directly or indirectly. Return the number of provinces.

cases.name: a 1,500 city chain
cases.code:
n = 1500
m = [[1 if abs(i - j) <= 1 else 0 for j in range(n)] for i in range(n)]
assert find_provinces(m) == 1

hints: Count connected components: run a search from every city not visited yet, and count how many searches you start.
A long chain makes recursion very deep. Use an explicit stack, or union-find, to stay safe.
notes: Union-find: O(n^2 * alpha(n)) because the input is an n by n matrix. DFS or BFS gives the same O(n^2). Mention that with an adjacency list the cost would be O(V + E).

title: K Closest Points to the Origin
statement: Given a list of points [x, y] and an integer k, return the k points closest to the origin (0, 0) by straight-line distance. The answer may be in any order and is unique apart from order.

cases.name: 100,000 points must be fast
cases.code:
pts = [[i, -i] for i in range(100000)]
assert sorted(k_closest(pts, 3)) == [[0, 0], [1, -1], [2, -2]]

hints: You do not need the square root: comparing x*x + y*y gives the same order.
Keep a max-heap of size k. Push each point, and when it grows past k, remove the farthest. Python heaps are min-heaps, so store the negative distance.
notes: Heap of size k: O(n log k) time, O(k) space. Sorting everything is O(n log n). Quickselect averages O(n) but is harder to write under pressure. Ask whether k is small or close to n.

title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
statement: Given a string of digits from 2 to 9, return all letter combinations the digits could represent on a phone keypad (2 = abc, 3 = def, 4 = ghi, 5 = jkl, 6 = mno, 7 = pqrs, 8 = tuv, 9 = wxyz). Return an empty list for an empty string. The order does not matter.
hints: Build the answer one digit at a time: for each letter of this digit, continue with the next digit.
Backtracking: choose a letter, recurse on the rest, undo the choice. When the path is as long as the input, save it.
notes: The output has up to 4^n strings, so O(4^n * n) time is unavoidable. Recursion depth is only n. Mention that the empty-input case returns [] and not [""].

title: Word Search
statement: Given a grid of letters and a word, return True if the word can be built from letters of sequentially adjacent cells (up, down, left, right). The same cell may not be used twice in one word.

cases.name: one cell
cases.code: assert exist([["A"]], "A") is True and exist([["A"]], "B") is False

cases.name: board is restored
cases.code:
b = [["A", "B"], ["C", "D"]]
assert exist(b, "ABDC") is True
assert b == [["A", "B"], ["C", "D"]]

hints: Start a depth-first search from every cell that matches the first letter.
Mark the cell as used while exploring (for example, replace it with "#") and restore it when you backtrack.
notes: Worst case O(rows * cols * 3^L) for a word of length L (three directions after the first step). Restoring the cell is the backtracking step interviewers watch for.

title: Word Break
statement: Given a string s and a list of words, return True if s can be split into a sequence of one or more words from the list. Words may be reused.
hints: dp[i] means: the first i characters can be split into words. dp[0] is True.
dp[i] is True if some j < i has dp[j] True and s[j:i] is a word. Put the words in a set.
notes: O(n * L) substring checks where L is the longest word (each slice costs up to L), O(n) space. Plain recursion without memoization is exponential: say that this is overlapping subproblems.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
statement: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence of nums. A subsequence keeps the order but may skip elements.
hints: A simple dp[i] = longest subsequence ending at i takes O(n^2).
For O(n log n) keep a list "tails" where tails[k] is the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1. Use binary search (bisect_left) to place each number.
notes: O(n log n) time, O(n) space. Present the O(n^2) dp first because it is easy to explain, then improve it. bisect_left gives strictly increasing (bisect_right would allow equal values). The tails list is not itself a valid subsequence.

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
statement: Given a list of positive integers, return True if it can be split into two subsets with the same sum.

cases.name: a big item makes it impossible

hints: The total must be even. The question becomes: is there a subset with sum total / 2?
This is 0/1 knapsack. Keep a boolean array reachable[s]. For each number, update from high sums to low so that a number is not used twice.
notes: O(n * target) time, O(target) space: pseudo-polynomial. The reverse loop is the detail: iterating upward would reuse the same number (unbounded knapsack).

title: Jump Game
statement: You start at index 0 of a list nums. nums[i] is the maximum number of steps you can jump forward from index i. Return True if you can reach the last index.

examples.note: every path ends at index 3, where the jump is 0

cases.name: zero in the middle is fine if jumped over

hints: Track the furthest index you can reach so far.
If the current index is beyond the furthest reach, you are stuck. If the furthest reach is at least the last index, return True.
notes: Greedy: O(n) time, O(1) space. A dp or backtracking solution is O(n^2) or exponential. The reason greedy is correct: if index i is reachable, so is every index before it that is within the furthest reach.

title: Trapping Rain Water
statement: Given a list of non-negative integers representing bar heights (each bar has width 1), return how much water is trapped between the bars after it rains.
hints: Water above a bar = min(tallest bar to its left, tallest bar to its right) - its height.
Two pointers: move the pointer with the smaller max, because that side is limited by its own max, not by the other side.
solution:
def trap(height):
    lo, hi = 0, len(height) - 1
    left_max = right_max = 0
    water = 0
    while lo < hi:
        if height[lo] < height[hi]:
            left_max = max(left_max, height[lo])
            water += left_max - height[lo]
            lo += 1
        else:
            right_max = max(right_max, height[hi])
            water += right_max - height[hi]
            hi -= 1
    return water
notes: Two pointers: O(n) time, O(1) space. State the O(n) space version first (prefix max and suffix max arrays), because it is easier to explain, then reduce the space.
